vignette:
Mateo has always been a man of stories. For thirty-five years, he built a life and a legacy around them, curating narratives as the owner of a small, respected publishing house. His hands, now spotted with age, have held the weight of countless manuscripts, each a world contained within its pages, with a clear beginning, a middle, and an end. His own story felt much the same: a steady, predictable narrative of hard work, a loving marriage to Leilani, and the quiet pride of a life well-lived on the island. That narrative was shattered two years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon.

The inter-island ferry was a routine he'd taken a hundred times, a mundane necessity for meetings on the main island. He remembers the weather was clear, the sea calm. He was reading a promising debut novel, the words crisp and orderly on the page. The first jolt was violent and wrong, not the familiar rock of the waves but a metallic, grinding scream from below. Then came the second, a sickening lurch that sent people and chairs sliding across the deck. The world dissolved into chaos. He remembers the smell of diesel fuel and salt water, a combination that now catches in his throat at unexpected times. He remembers the cacophony of panicked shouts, a sound that held no individual words, only pure terror. He remembers the cold shock of the water, the desperate gasp for air, and the image that is now seared behind his eyes: a small, red child's shoe, floating untethered on the churning surface of the water.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani treated him as if he were made of glass. The community rallied, but their sympathy felt distant, a language he no longer understood. He tried to return to work, to the familiar comfort of his office, but the words on the page would no longer stay still. They would swim and blur, the black ink bleeding into the dark water of his memory. He would be editing a sentence about a character's journey, and suddenly he would be back in the ocean, the weight of his waterlogged clothes pulling him down, the red shoe bobbing just out of reach. He started missing deadlines, his famous attention to detail completely gone.

Now, at sixty-three, Mateo is a ghost in his own life. Sleep offers no escape; it is a treacherous country populated by nightmares of the sinking, of faces he couldn't save. He wakes up gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs, the sheets damp with sweat. Leilani has taken to sleeping with a hand on his back, as if to anchor him to the present. During the day, he is a sentry, perpetually on guard. The backfire of a truck sends a jolt of raw adrenaline through him. The sound of a crowd, even a happy one at the market, feels suffocating, the noise pressing in on him until he has to leave.

He has abandoned the rituals that once defined him. The evening walks with Leilani along the shoreline are a thing of the past; he cannot bear to look at the ocean, let alone smell the salt on the air. He takes the long road into town to avoid even a glimpse of the harbor. The publishing house, his life's work, is floundering. He sits at his desk for hours, staring at a manuscript, unable to connect with the story. The joy he once found in language is gone, replaced by a flat, gray emptiness. He feels an immense distance from everyone, especially Leilani. He sees her worry, feels her love, but it's as if he's watching it through a thick wall of ice. Underneath it all is a corrosive guilt. Why was he the one to grab a floating piece of wreckage? Why him, and not the woman whose child wore the little red shoe? It is a question with no answer, a story with no resolution, a manuscript he can neither edit nor discard.
